claims.claim: The Kasekela community of chimpanzees at Gombe National Park took over the territory of the neighbouring Kahama community after a series of lethal attacks.
claims.source: For instance, Goodall, 1986 famously documented how the Kasekela community of chimpanzees at Gombe National Park took over the territory of the neighbouring Kahama community after a series of lethal attacks.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a famous observational study.

claims.claim: Groups may lose part of their territory to a stronger neighbour in rattling cisticolas, vervet monkeys, chowchillas, and lions.
claims.source: More commonly, a group may lose part of its territory to a stronger neighbour, as seen in rattling cisticolas (Cisticola chiniana), vervet monkeys (Chlorocebus pygerythrus), chowchillas (Orthonyx spaldingii), and lions (Carlson, 1986; Isbell et al., 1990; Jansen, 1999; Mosser and Packer, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to observational studies across multiple species.

claims.claim: Reduced access to valuable resources has negative impacts on reproductive success in mud crabs, Seychelles warblers, and chimpanzees.
claims.source: Reduced access to valuable resources could also have negative impacts on both current and future reproductive success, as documented for mud crabs (Panopeus herbstii), Seychelles warblers (Acrocephalus sechellensis), and chimpanzees (Griffen and Norelli, 2015; Komdeur and Edelaar, 2001; Thompson et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies documenting reproductive consequences.

claims.claim: In Seychelles warblers and Florida scrub jays, sons can 'bud' off part of the territory and begin reproducing independently.
claims.source: One further benefit of increasing territory size in some bird species, such as Seychelles warblers and Florida scrub jays, is that sons can 'bud' off part of the territory and so begin reproducing independently (Komdeur and Edelaar, 2001; Stallcup and Woolfenden, 1978).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to observational studies.

claims.claim: Chronic stress is associated with reduced body condition and increased chances of mortality.
claims.source: Chronic stress is associated with reduced body condition and increased chances of mortality (Campos et al., 2021; Pride, 2005; Wey et al., 2014) due to, for example, increased susceptibility to predation (Romero et al., 2009; Vuarin et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on chronic stress effects.

claims.claim: Chronic stress may reduce reproductive investment and success through negative effects on courtship activity, breeding rates, fecundity, egg size and composition, and hatching and fledging success.
claims.source: Chronic stress may also reduce reproductive investment and success: it can have negative effects on courtship activity (Romero-Diaz et al., 2019; Schreck, 2010), breeding rates (Dulude‐de Broin et al., 2020; Mileva et al., 2011), fecundity (O'Brien et al., 2018; Schreck, 2010), egg size and composition (Ensminger et al., 2018; Henriksen et al., 2013), and hatching and fledging success (Cyr and Michael Romero, 2007; Eriksen et al., 2015; Kleist et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies documenting various reproductive effects.

claims.claim: An increased cumulative pressure from intergroup conflict is correlated with longer inter-birth intervals and reduced offspring survival in chimpanzees.
claims.source: A recent observational study on chimpanzees found that an increased cumulative pressure from intergroup conflict is correlated with longer inter-birth intervals and reduced offspring survival (Lemoine et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to an observational study.

claims.claim: An increase in outgroup threat can drive longer inter-clutch intervals, cause females to produce relatively smaller eggs with less protein, and result in fewer offspring surviving to one month post-hatching in cichlid fish.
claims.source: Experimental work with cichlid fish has demonstrated that an increase in outgroup threat can drive longer inter-clutch intervals, cause females to produce relatively smaller eggs with less protein, and result in fewer offspring surviving to one month post-hatching (Braga Goncalves & Radford, In revision).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to experimental work.

claims.claim: Outgroup threat has been found to be correlated with reduced foetal mortality in crested macaques and banded mongooses.
claims.source: The consequences are not necessarily always negative, however, as outgroup threat has been found to be correlated with reduced foetal mortality in crested macaques (Macaca nigra) and banded mongooses (Kerhoas et al., 2014; Thompson et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to observational studies.

claims.claim: Outgroup threat is correlated with increased pup survival in dwarf mongooses.
claims.source: and with increased pup survival in dwarf mongooses (Morris-Drake, 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study.

claims.claim: Offspring from smaller eggs and those with higher levels of corticosterone might be smaller, be of lower quality, and have learning difficulties.
claims.source: In general, offspring from smaller eggs and those with, for example, higher levels of corticosterone might be smaller, be of lower quality, and have learning difficulties (Dantzer et al., 2019; McCormick, 1998; Roche et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on maternal effects.

claims.claim: Early-life stress on offspring and lower growth has lasting effects on adult physiology and behaviour, with major effects on survival and reproductive success.
claims.source: Moreover, early-life stress on offspring and lower growth has lasting effects: there is increasing evidence that developmental trajectories shape the physiology and behaviour of adults, with major effects on survival and reproductive success (Cram et al., 2017; English et al., 2013; Marshall et al., 2017; Noguera et al., 2017; Royle et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies on developmental effects.

claims.claim: Conflict with whole groups likely has fitness consequences for all group members to a greater or lesser extent.
claims.source: Most obviously, conflict with whole groups likely has fitness consequences for all group members to a greater or lesser extent
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about the nature of whole-group conflict.

claims.claim: Conflict with a single outsider seeking breeding opportunities likely carries particularly high costs for one or a subset of group members.
claims.source: By contrast, conflict with a single outsider seeking breeding opportunities (Balshine et al., 1998; Lardy et al., 2015; Young et al., 2007) likely carries particularly high costs for one or a subset of group members
claims.evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to studies on individual outsider conflicts.

claims.claim: Intergroup conflict typically involves repeated interactions between the same groups of conspecifics, often in specific contested areas.
claims.source: Moreover, whilst intergroup conflict typically involves repeated interactions between the same groups of conspecifics, often in specific (contested) areas (Radford, 2010)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study.

claims.claim: In green woodhoopoes, most intergroup contests are resolved through vocal signalling and thus do not result in deaths.
claims.source: For example, in species such as green woodhoopoes, most intergroup contests are resolved through vocal signalling and thus do not result in deaths (Radford, 2003)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to an observational study.

claims.claim: Interactions between rival banded mongoose groups usually escalate into physical combat, with 10% of adult and 20% of juvenile deaths attributed to this cause.
claims.source: in striking contrast, interactions between rival banded mongoose groups usually escalate into physical combat, with 10% of adult and 20% of juvenile deaths attributed to this cause (Johnstone et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation with specific quantitative data.

claims.claim: In lions, dominant groups have higher-quality territories, which are associated with greater female reproductive success.
claims.source: In lions, for example, dominant groups have higher-quality territories, which are associated with greater female reproductive success (Mosser and Packer, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to an observational study.

claims.claim: In acacia ants, victors in contests expend valuable time and energy and may lose resource-holding capacity, meaning a reduced ability to defend themselves from predators, parasites or subsequent attacks.
claims.source: Moreover, winners may suffer important costs, as evidenced in acacia ants (Crematogaster mimosae): in outlasting or killing rivals, victors expend valuable time and energy and may lose resource-holding capacity (i.e. suffer their own losses in numbers), meaning a reduced ability to defend themselves from predators, parasites or subsequent attacks from conspecifics (Rudolph and McEntee, 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a study documenting costs to winners.

claims.claim: Aggressive intergroup interactions in banded mongooses may be initiated by females moving into the territory of a neighbouring group, where females may gain extra-group matings whilst their own-group males are distracted in battle.
claims.source: For instance, aggressive intergroup interactions in banded mongooses may be initiated by females moving into the territory of a neighbouring group; the females may gain extra-group matings whilst their own-group males are distracted in battle and suffer the physical costs of the contest (Johnstone et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to an observational study.

claims.claim: Sex differences in regulation of the vertebrate hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal/interrenal axes mean that there are likely differences in how males and females respond to the stress of outgroup conflict.
claims.source: In terms of chronic effects, sex differences in regulation of the vertebrate hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal/interrenal axes (Young et al., 2007) mean that there are likely differences in how males and females respond to the stress of outgroup conflict (Culbert et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations and involves inference about sex differences in stress response.

claims.claim: Theoretical modelling of outgroup conflict has mainly focused on the determinants of group success in contests, individual variation in participation, and demographic influences on costs and benefits of involvement.
claims.source: To date, theoretical modelling of outgroup conflict has mainly focused on the determinants of group success in contests (Franks and Partridge, 1993; Johnson and MacKay, 2015), individual variation in participation (Gavrilets and Fortunato, 2014; Schindler and Radford, 2018), and demographic influences on costs and benefits of involvement (Lehmann, 2011; see Rusch and Gavrilets, 2020 for a review).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to theoretical work.

claims.claim: A formal theoretical framework integrating the key factors determining the fitness consequences of outgroup conflict, incorporating cumulative as well as immediate consequences, is yet to be created.
claims.source: A formal theoretical framework integrating the key factors determining the fitness consequences of outgroup conflict, incorporating cumulative as well as immediate consequences, is yet to be created.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claims.claim: Long-term datasets from individually identifiable wild animals offer a particularly valuable window into fitness consequences of outgroup conflict.
claims.source: Because outgroup interactions occur repeatedly, and their effects can be cumulative and transgenerational, long-term datasets from individually identifiable wild animals (Clutton-Brock and Sheldon, 2010) offer a particularly valuable window into fitness consequences (Kerhoas et al., 2014; Lemoine et al., 2020; Thompson et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to long-term studies and a general citation about the value of such datasets.

results.result: The authors establish that while outgroup conflict is recognized as a powerful selection pressure, empirical studies quantifying fitness consequences have focused narrowly on immediate effects from physical contests, with traditional research emphasizing behavior during contests.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, and C5 are well-supported by citations to the existing literature and represent an accurate characterization of the field's historical focus. The authors provide specific exceptions (C2) which strengthens the claim about the general pattern.

results.result: Outgroup conflict from conspecific outsiders threatening valuable resources occurs across a broad taxonomic range, and theoretical work indicates its selective importance in evolution of within-group dynamics, cooperation, territoriality, and social structure.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C4 are supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 1 demonstrating taxonomic breadth. These establish the widespread nature and theoretical importance of outgroup conflict as foundational context for the review.

results.result: The authors argue that fitness consequences of outgroup conflict extend beyond immediate costs from physical violence to include effects from secondary cues of rival presence and overall outgroup threat, which can produce behavioral and hormonal changes that translate into fitness consequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 present a logical progression supported by citations, drawing an analogy to predation effects (C7). The inference from behavioral/hormonal effects to fitness consequences (C9) is reasonable though the authors appropriately use conditional language ('could translate').

results.result: The authors establish that outgroup conflict can have knock-on consequences affecting fitness of both directly involved individuals and third-party group members across current and subsequent generations, with differential effects on different individuals including both positive and negative consequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C13 are well-supported by citations documenting various knock-on and transgenerational effects. The example of breeding position takeover (C13) effectively illustrates how the same event has different fitness consequences for different individuals.

results.result: Outgroup contests can result in immediate mortality through targeted killing or as by-products of escalated contests, affecting adults, offspring, and specific vulnerable individuals across diverse taxa including termites, mongooses, primates, and birds.
results.evaluation: Claims C16, C17, C40, and C41 document targeted killing with appropriate citations, while C18-C20 provide examples of other immediate contest outcomes. Each claim is supported by citations to observational studies across different taxa.

results.result: Extra-group mating during outgroup conflict occurs through two main mechanisms: males roving between groups seeking mating opportunities (alpine marmots, meerkats) and individuals sneaking matings while others are occupied in contests (banded mongooses, common marmosets).
results.evaluation: Claims C43, C44, and C18 are each supported by citations to observational studies documenting these mating strategies. The organization into two distinct mechanisms is logical and well-supported.

results.result: Breeder takeovers by outsiders occur across many taxa including primates, carnivores, ungulates, rodents, and birds, with examples showing coalitions can be more successful than lone individuals.
results.evaluation: Claim C45 is supported by multiple citations across diverse taxa and reference to Figure 2. Claim C20 provides a specific example with citation. The taxonomic breadth is well-documented.

results.result: Physical confrontations with outsiders can lead to injuries across a wide range of species, and injured animals likely have greater mortality rates and reduced reproductive performance.
results.evaluation: Claim C46 is supported by extensive citations across diverse taxa. Claim C47 is supported by citations on injury consequences. Claim C21 provides a specific example. The inference about fitness consequences of injury (C47) is reasonable and citation-supported.

results.result: Lethal fights can create breeding vacancies benefiting subordinate group members, with evidence that in some species (dry wood termites) non-breeders may actively incite conflicts to increase the likelihood of breeder mortality.
results.evaluation: Claim C48 is supported by citation documenting this pattern. Claim C49 presents an unusual case with appropriate citation and cautious language ('believed to'), acknowledging the speculative nature of the proposed mechanism.

results.result: Breeder takeovers can benefit opposite-sex group members by providing access to unrelated mates, with evidence from geladas showing accelerated sexual maturation in subordinate females following male takeovers and meerkats showing increased reproduction when unrelated males are present.
results.evaluation: Claims C50 and C28 are supported by citations to studies with temporal and observational data respectively. These document positive fitness consequences for some third-party individuals following breeder changes.

results.result: Newly established breeding pairings following takeovers may produce fewer offspring compared to long-established pairs, as documented in alpine marmots, Azara's owl monkeys, and pied babblers.
results.evaluation: Claim C51 is supported by citations to three species showing this pattern. This documents a negative fitness consequence for remaining breeders following partner replacement.

results.result: Incoming male breeders in multiple species kill dependent offspring to bring females into estrus sooner, and females may exhibit higher abortion rates and reduced fertility following takeovers, with quantified effects including 3.5 month delays in conception (lions) and 32-fold increases in infant mortality (geladas).
results.evaluation: Claims C52 and C53 are supported by multiple citations documenting infanticide and reproductive effects. Claims C29 and C30 provide specific quantitative data from cited studies, strengthening the evidence for these fitness consequences.

results.result: Incoming breeders sometimes evict existing group members including former breeders, other adults, and independent offspring, with evidence from cichlids, Florida scrub-jays, Arabian babblers, and African lions showing that evicted individuals, particularly young males, often experience premature death.
results.evaluation: Claims C54, C31, and C36 are each supported by citations to observational studies documenting eviction behavior and its consequences across different taxa. The fitness costs of eviction are well-documented.

results.result: Individuals that are evicted or leave groups suffer fitness consequences because being alone or in small splinter groups results in increased predation, reduced foraging success, and fatal encounters with rivals, with clear evidence from lions and meerkats showing negative effects on longevity.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 is supported by citations documenting various consequences of group departure. Claim C56 provides specific evidence from two species with data on longevity effects, strengthening the general claim.

results.result: Changes in group size from outgroup conflict affect fitness through multiple pathways: relative group size influences contest outcomes (meerkats, green woodhoopoes), helper loss reduces reproductive success in cooperative breeders, and specific examples show territory loss and increased vulnerability following groupmate death (spotted hyenas) and benefits from brood raiding (ants).
results.evaluation: Claims C57 and C58 are supported by citations documenting the importance of group size. Claims C32 and C33 provide specific examples with citations. The connection between group size changes and fitness is well-established.

results.result: Close encounters with outsiders and inspection of rival cues can lead to disease and parasite transmission, with social stress increasing susceptibility, and infected or parasitized animals experiencing increased mortality and reduced reproductive output, as exemplified by Varroa mite transmission in honeybees and modeled for African lions.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C63 form a logical chain supported by citations at each step. Claim C22 provides a specific documented example of parasite transmission. Claim C60 adds modeling evidence. The pathway from contact to disease to fitness consequences is well-supported.

results.result: Interactions with rivals and their cues result in behavioral changes including altered space use, increased defensive behaviors, and changes in movement patterns, with experimental evidence from dwarf mongooses showing increased scent-marking, vigilance, and grooming in response to rival feces, and observational data showing losing groups avoid conflict areas (baboons) or increase movement (capuchins).
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by citations to both experimental (C65) and observational (C64, C66) studies. Claims C23 and C24 provide specific examples with temporal and behavioral data. The evidence for behavioral responses is strong.

results.result: Cumulative outgroup pressure can lead to changes in territory ownership or size, ranging from complete takeover (Gombe chimpanzees) to partial loss (multiple species), with documented negative impacts on reproductive success from reduced resource access and positive benefits for winners including territory budding opportunities in some bird species, and experimental evidence from ants showing up to 35% territory loss following colony size reduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C70 are supported by citations including a famous case study (C67) and examples across taxa (C68). Claim C69 documents fitness consequences with citations. Claim C25 provides experimental evidence with quantitative data. Claim C70 identifies a specific benefit.

results.result: Cumulative outgroup threat generates chronic stress with documented survival and reproductive consequences including reduced body condition, increased mortality, and negative effects on courtship, breeding rates, fecundity, and egg quality, with observational evidence from chimpanzees showing correlations between intergroup conflict pressure and longer inter-birth intervals/reduced offspring survival, experimental evidence from cichlids demonstrating causal effects on reproductive parameters, and physiological data showing elevated cortisol in chimpanzees on days with intergroup encounters.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 are supported by extensive citations documenting stress effects. Claims C73-C74 provide specific evidence from observational (chimpanzees) and experimental (cichlids) studies. Claims C26-C27 add physiological and fitness data. The evidence spans multiple levels from mechanism to consequence.

results.result: Outgroup threat can have positive fitness consequences in some cases, with correlations found between outgroup threat and reduced fetal mortality in crested macaques and banded mongooses, and increased pup survival in dwarf mongooses.
results.evaluation: Claims C75 and C76 are supported by citations to observational studies. These document important exceptions to the general pattern of negative consequences, though the mechanisms are not explained. The correlational nature is appropriately noted.

results.result: Outgroup conflict has transgenerational fitness consequences through maternal effects and reduced parental care, with offspring from smaller eggs or with elevated stress hormones showing reduced size, quality, and learning difficulties, and early-life stress having lasting effects on adult physiology and behavior affecting survival and reproductive success, as documented in pied babblers (reduced reproductive success from nest neglect during territory defense), crested macaques (tripled infant mortality after takeovers), chimpanzees (reduced infant survival with high neighbor pressure during pregnancy), and cichlids (lower offspring survivorship and smaller body size under chronic conflict).
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 establish general principles supported by citations. Claims C34, C35, C37, C38 provide specific examples with quantitative data from cited studies. Claim C39 links offspring size to future fitness in cichlids. The evidence for transgenerational effects is strong across multiple pathways and taxa.

results.result: The authors argue that different types of outgroup conflict generate different selection pressures: conflict with whole groups affects all members and involves repeated interactions in specific areas, while conflict with individual outsiders carries particularly high costs for specific individuals and varies more in location and identity of competitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 present logical inferences about how conflict type affects fitness consequences. Claim C81 is supported by citation. The distinctions drawn are reasonable and important for understanding selection pressures, though somewhat conceptual.

results.result: Interspecific variation in outgroup conflict frequency and intensity influences fitness consequences, with examples ranging from green woodhoopoes where most contests are resolved vocally without deaths, to banded mongooses where 10-20% of deaths are attributed to intergroup combat, and evidence that even winners can suffer costs (acacia ants losing resource-holding capacity) while dominant groups may have fitness benefits (lions with higher-quality territories).
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are each supported by citations providing specific examples with quantitative data (C83, C84). These effectively illustrate the range of variation in conflict intensity and consequences across species.

results.result: Within groups, different individuals experience different fitness consequences from the same outgroup event, with evidence from banded mongooses showing females may initiate conflicts to gain extra-group matings while males suffer physical costs, and sex differences in stress axis regulation suggesting males and females respond differently to outgroup conflict stress.
results.evaluation: Claim C86 is supported by citation to an observational study documenting sex-specific strategies and costs. Claim C87 is supported by citations and involves reasonable inference about sex differences in stress response based on physiological differences.

results.result: The authors identify a gap in theoretical work, noting that while existing models have focused on determinants of contest success, individual participation variation, and demographic influences, a formal theoretical framework integrating key factors determining fitness consequences and incorporating cumulative as well as immediate consequences has yet to be created.
results.evaluation: Claim C88 is supported by citations to existing theoretical work. Claim C89 identifies the gap based on the authors' assessment of the field. This represents an accurate characterization of the current state of theory.

results.result: The authors argue that long-term datasets from individually identifiable wild animals offer particularly valuable windows into fitness consequences of outgroup conflict because interactions occur repeatedly and effects can be cumulative and transgenerational.
results.evaluation: Claim C90 is supported by citations to long-term studies that have successfully documented fitness consequences and a general citation about the value of such datasets. The argument is logical given the temporal nature of the effects described earlier.

results.result: The authors note increasing recognition that not all interactions with conspecific outsiders entail conflict, with bonobos showing many peaceful intergroup encounters, though they acknowledge their review focuses primarily on conflict perspectives.
results.evaluation: Claims C14 and C15 are supported by citations, with C15 including a caveat citation suggesting debate. The authors appropriately acknowledge this complexity while justifying their focus on conflict.

results.result: The authors suggest that engagement in fighting behavior may incur increased predation risk as participants are distracted, though this is presented as a possibility rather than established fact.
results.evaluation: Claim C42 is supported by citations but uses cautious language ('possibility'). The citations suggest this effect but it appears less well-established than other fitness consequences described. More direct evidence would strengthen this claim.
